Guessing how many people Saturday needs is expensive either way.

Too high and you pay people to stand around. Too low and the team is flat out while customers wait.

This week Shiftbase launched Auto-scheduling for shift-based businesses. An AI forecast predicts how busy each department will be, up to 28 days ahead, from revenue history, the weather and the calendar. Labour demand turns that into how many people you need each hour. Then Auto-scheduling drafts the roster across departments and locations against availability, skills, contract hours and labour cost.

You still check it and publish. Nothing reaches the team before that.

That timing matters for more than cafes:

A cleaning contractor who knows which sites will be short before the week starts.
A hotel that staffs the busy Saturday from its own history, not last year's gut feel.
A facilities team that sees the unfilled skill gap as a hiring question, not a last-minute scramble.

Forecast the demand, draft the roster, then decide. The admin shrinks; the judgement stays with you.

At iQCheckPoint we see the same idea in live rostering and timesheets: get the right person in the right place, and keep the record clean as the week runs.

How do top Indian IT service companies adjust their business models to handle higher prevailing wage requirements for H-1B visas?

Top Indian IT service companies (such as TCS, Infosys, Wipro, and HCLTech) have spent the past several years aggressively shifting their business strategies to mitigate the impact of tighter H-1B visa rules and higher prevailing wage requirements set by the U.S. Department of Labor (DOL).

Traditionally, the Indian IT model relied on deploying junior-to-mid-level software engineers to client sites in the U.S. at Wage Level I (entry-level) or Wage Level II (qualified/mid-level) salaries. As regulatory pressure increased wage floors and favored higher-paying roles in selection lotteries, IT providers adapted through structural business model shifts.

1. Slashing H-1B Dependence & Sharply Reducing Petitions
Instead of relying heavily on new H-1B petitions, Indian IT leaders have dramatically curtailed their new visa filings.
- Massive Drops in Filings: Major IT services firms cut initial H-1B filings by over 40% to 50% across five-year periods. Recent cap-season registration data shows companies like Infosys, TCS, and Cognizant reducing initial petition registrations significantly compared to historic highs.
- Transitioning to High-End Filings Only: For the H-1B petitions they do file, companies focus almost exclusively on specialized, senior, or architect roles that naturally qualify for Level III or Level IV prevailing wage rates. This ensures higher petition approval odds and reduces friction during U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) reviews.

2. Expanding Onsite Local Hiring (U.S. Delivery Centers)
To maintain project continuity without paying foreign visa overhead, Indian tech giants shifted heavily toward localized U.S. workforces.
- Local Delivery Hubs: Companies established delivery centers in cities across Texas, Indiana, North Carolina, and Ohio to hire U.S. citizens, green card holders, and local STEM university graduates.
- Campus Recruiting & Reskilling: Rather than sponsoring offshore talent at Level I prevailing wages, IT firms now hire local American graduates and run intensive internal bootcamp programs to bridge skill gaps at market-rate domestic salaries.

3. Global Capability Centers (GCCs) & Offshore Delivery
Instead of bringing workers to the client's country, Indian IT companies are increasingly encouraging clients to move the work to where the talent is.
- The GCC Explosion in India: Multinational enterprise clients are establishing or expanding their own Global Capability Centers (GCCs) directly in India (in hubs like Bengaluru, Hyderabad, and Pune). Indian IT companies act as strategic partners to set up, staff, and manage these onshore/offshore operations.
- Near-shoring Hubs: For U.S. clients who require real-time time-zone alignment, Indian providers expanded delivery hubs in Canada and Latin America (Mexico, Costa Rica, Brazil), using favorable local work authorization frameworks instead of U.S. visas.

4. Alternative Executive & Intra-Company Visas (L-1A / L-1B)
To bypass the H-1B lottery system and prevailing wage restrictions altogether, IT firms rely more heavily on alternative visa routes:
- L-1 Visas (Intra-Company Transferees): Employees who have worked at the company’s Indian offices for at least one continuous year are transferred to U.S. branches via L-1A (Managers/Executives) or L-1B (Specialized Knowledge) visas.
- L-1 Advantage: L-1 visas are not subject to the annual H-1B lottery cap and do not mandate the same rigid prevailing wage scale filings as the H-1B program.

5. Transitioning from "Time & Materials" to Outcome-Based Pricing
Higher wage floors directly shrink profit margins under traditional "Time & Materials" contracts (where clients pay a fixed hourly rate per deployed onsite engineer).

To protect operating margins:
- Fixed-Price & Outcome-Based Contracts: Firms have shifted client billing to managed services, fixed-fee deliverables, or platform-driven service models.
- AI & Automation Integration: By integrating Generative AI, automated testing, and low-code tools into client delivery, IT providers reduce the absolute headcount required onsite—allowing them to pay higher wages to a smaller team of senior leaders without eroding project profitability.

Ask any in-house Head of Production what frustrates them most after hiring an external freelancer or agency for a short-term project, and you will hear the same story:

"The final MP4 looked great—but when we needed to change one headline two weeks later, we couldn't open their project file, half the fonts were missing, and the AI workflow was a complete black box."

When a company brings in a specialist for a 2-to-3-month contract, the true test of professionalism isn't just what happens on launch day. It’s what happens the day AFTER the contract ends.

On every short-term engagement we take on, we follow a strict "Zero Black-Box Handover Standard" so the internal team owns 100% of the capability:

1. Color-Coded, Self-Explanatory Master Timelines:
Every Adobe Premiere Pro, After Effects, and DaVinci Resolve project is scrubbed of broken links, collected with all active footage/fonts, and color-coded by track (Blue for locked picture, Emerald for voice/foley, Amber for editable typography, Violet for adjustment LUTs).

2. Separated Alpha Sprites & Open Prompt Documentation:
We never hand over flattened, uneditable renders if a layer might need updating. All product cutouts, #FFFFFF knolling prop sheets, 3x3 character turnarounds, and optical prompt structures are organized in a clean, human-readable folder tree.

3. The 15-Minute Loom Walkthrough:
Along with the final master drive, we record a calm, 15-minute screen walkthrough showing the in-house editors exactly how the comps are rigged and how to swap languages or ratios in five minutes.

True confidence as a creative specialist means never hoarding your process to force a client to depend on you. Share your systems generously—clients always remember the partner who empowered their team.

"AI will inevitably replace your job" has got to be the laziest prediction in business right now.

I hear it in a number of leadership conversations I have. It gets nodded along to in board papers, thrown around in the media, and repeated so often that nobody stops to check if it's actually true.

DBS Bank — one of Singapore's largest banks — just showed what the alternative looks like at real scale: 13,000 people, one AI-augmented transformation. Redundancies: zero.

How did they do it? Their Group HR Head set one guiding principle for the entire transformation: protect people, not jobs.

That's an important distinction. Protecting a job means freezing a role in place and quietly hoping AI never gets to it. Protecting a person means redesigning the role around what they're genuinely good at, and building a real pathway to what's next.

DBS didn't run redundancies. They stopped hiring into roles AI was absorbing, and let around 4,000 temporary and contract positions run off naturally over three years — instead of cutting permanent people loose.

Frontline roles didn't shrink — they got rebuilt. AI took on the admin sitting around each customer interaction. People kept the part of the job that was always the actual point: reading the customer, solving the problem, making the call a machine can't make.

That's the real fork in the road with AI. Frame it as a headcount story, and you get fear, disengagement, and people quietly updating their CVs.

Frame it as a capability story, and you get momentum.

— Garry Green, Managing Director and Founder, Quanton

A technology company in Hangzhou ended a supervisor's contract after he refused a lower post. Only in arbitration did it give the reason: AI could now do his job. An arbitration panel, a district court and the Hangzhou Intermediate People's Court all found the dismissal unlawful. The company owed him more than Rmb 260,000 in damages.

For companies running AI programs in China, the layoff rules matter too. Article 41 of China's Labor Contract Law covers layoffs of 20 or more people, or of 10% or more of the workforce. The employer must explain to the union or all staff 30 days in advance and report the plan to the labor authority. Below that threshold, the reporting procedure does not apply.

Cutting a few people at a time avoids the report. My latest analysis finds that, in AI cases like the three it reviews, a smaller round does not give the firm a cheaper legal ground.

For employers and investors, the open question is the hires a firm does not make. My piece reads China's new State Council document on AI and employment against that question, and sets it beside hiring data from China and the US.

Spending on AI and being AI native are two different things, and two numbers that keep getting mixed up prove it.

The first number comes from Anthropic's S-1. As of September 30, 2026, Anthropic has more than 11,900 customers spending $100K or more a year. More than 1,900 spend $1M or more, and about 250 spend $10M or more.

The second number is my own thesis: there are only about 17,000 truly AI-native firms in the world. Here's how I get there. Start with 3.55 billion employed people. About 0.2% of them actually work AI native, which is 7.1 million people. About 4% of those employ others, which is 284,000. About 6% of those employ 20 or more people. That leaves roughly 17,000 firms.

Because 11,900 and 17,000 sit in the same range, people assume they describe the same companies. They don't. They're two different lists with some overlap. Treating them as one hides the most useful insight in the whole filing.

A lot of the big spenders are large enterprises buying access. They have the budget, the procurement process and the seat licenses. A lot of the AI-native firms are small. They spend less, but they build more. Their workflows, their roles and their margins are designed around agents from the start.

So here's my takeaway. Spending on AI doesn't make you AI native. Building with it does. A $1M contract with a lab can still sit on top of an org chart that works exactly the way it did five years ago. Meanwhile a 25-person firm with a modest bill can be running half of its operations through agents.

The difference shows up in the details. In an AI-native firm, a single operator might manage several agents that handle research, drafting, reporting and follow-up. In a company that is only spending, the same tools often sit in a browser tab that people open when they remember to. Both show up as customers. Only one has actually changed how the work gets done.

This is what we're building toward at Single Grain and with Single Brain, our AI-native operating system where operators run agents and bots as part of how the work actually gets done.

If you want to move from spending on AI to building with it, here's the path I'd take:

1. Stop measuring AI adoption by seats or spend and start measuring it by workflows that run with agents.
2. Pick one revenue-critical process and redesign it from scratch as if agents were available on day one.
3. Give every team lead one agent they own, maintain and improve each month.
4. Hire people who have already built with AI, and ask them in interviews to show you something they automated.
5. Review your org chart every quarter and ask which roles are now operators of agents rather than doers of tasks.

We're hiring AI-native people at singlegrain.com/careers.

From my Leveling Up S-1 series.

Be honest: is your company on the spending list, the building list, or both?

Reflecting on 2026... I have mixed feelings. It has been a tough year, dare I say the toughest since COVID... possibly since 2008 Financial Crisis?!

Here are the facts; In the 20 years I have been doing Risk Recruitment, it has always been a client driven market (i.e. there are more candidates than jobs)... Except in 2022- but that's a story for another day.

This year is the same. There are quite simply more jobs than candidates - this is something we are used to - so why so difficult? 

1) Cost pressures - yes these are evident year on year - this year is no different
2) Reduction in buy side fees - Yes again this has been incremental and this year is no different.
3) M&A Activity - consolidation in the industry, less jobs.


What's changed?
4) Cautious economies, fragile following knocks from political landscapes and war-impacted financial markets.
5) America first - Whilst not policy, it has certainly been a phenomena that where companies have a US Counterparty, head-of roles have migrated west from the UK.
6) AI - Is this as big as Dot.com? Technical revolution or evolution? It certainly seems to have more hype than any other technical advance before it - but in risk, we haven't seen too many lost jobs... yet?!

The impact: 15-20% of the Investment Risk Heads in the UK are unemployed. Up from a benchmark of 5% usually.

There is fantastic talent, just sitting there waiting for a job; contract, daily rate or perm - take your pick, the hiring manager is a good position... however, candidates are frustrated with long processes and nuanced roles which seem to take longer than necessary.

That being said, looking the hard numbers - what I invoice at the end of the day is up on last year (and the year before, and the year before that)...Why?

In all honesty, I owe this entirely to fantastic clients who have trusted me (often exclusively) to deliver the best solution to their challenges- I couldn't do it without you! (not forgetting the frequent late nights and what seemed to be blood sweat and tears which poured into every search!)

In short, an extraordinarily tough year finishing on a high due to exceptional people. Thank you to my market, clients, candidates and colleagues who have offered me the opportunity to work with them.

Lastly, 2026 is not over yet: I have active vacancies across:

Investment Risk - Mid & Senior levels
Commodities Market Risk - Oil & Energy, Mid & Senior levels
AI Model natural language training - All levels within finance (5+ years experience needed)


Looking ahead to 2027... Please send me your hiring mandates! My team and I will continue to offer professional, effective solutions to ensure the most efficient process tailored to you!

Our latest SAPQ1 Market Report is now live for our full network

The market is moving, but not everyone is moving at the same speed.
In this quarter's report we share what we're seeing across the SAP market, both subjective and objectively including:

The outlook for the next 6 to 12 months
AI and is it really having an effect
The SAP skills currently in demand
Contract rate movements over the past three years

The consistent theme from our conversations with clients and candidates is that organisations want to do more with less. Budgets remain tight and hiring decisions are taking longer so we have brought together insights from across our SAP recruitment team to give you a genuine view of what's happening on the coal face.

(5 minute read)

Are we acquiring AI capability or surrendering strategic control? The choice to buy model APIs, spin up owned compute, or outsource everything is the infrastructure decision that will define our company’s AI sovereignty — and its balance sheet — for a decade.

As a CTO I've seen teams rush to the latest API for speed and then discover they traded away latency, data control, and negotiating leverage. Here’s a practical framework I use when advising exec teams:

- Start with needs: classify data sensitivity, latency requirements, and expected scale.
- Short horizon (MVP/time-to-market): prefer third-party APIs with strict contract terms, private endpoints, and clear data use clauses.
- Medium/long horizon (scale, IP, regulated data): plan owned or dedicated compute; model stewardship becomes strategic.
- Recognize vendor lock-in costs: integration complexity, contract exit costs, and hiring for specific platforms.
- Hybrid by design: prototype on APIs, instrument for portability, and stage investments in compute once TCO and talent align.

Governance matters: define an AI infrastructure committee, require exit-readiness in contracts, and bake observability into every integration. Treat this decision like real estate — location, control, and long-term costs matter.
